proof:
# A global two-branch inverse for a tetrahedral centroid with one noncentral coordinate

Let b=(a,c,g,d) have positive coordinates summing to 1, with

    a>1/3, c<=1/3, g<1/3, d<1/3.

Fix the strict quadrilateral split {1,2}|{3,4}, oriented toward vertex 1. There are at most TWO unoriented section planes of the probability tetrahedron with this split and actual section centroid b. This holds with arbitrary unequal coordinates and includes c=1/3.

More precisely, all such sections correspond bijectively to the roots of one strictly convex scalar function H(K)=1 on an explicitly given interval. That function diverges to infinity at both ends. There are therefore zero, one double, or two simple solutions. This is a global inverse-section theorem, not a proof that three sections using DIFFERENT splits cannot be positively balanced, and not an OC theorem.

## 1. Exact inverse coordinates and the admissible interval

Set

    A=3a-1>0, B=3c-1<=0,
    G=1-3g>0, D=1-3d>0,
    U=A+B, V=AB, W=GD, delta=W-V.

Here B>-1, G,D<1, and G+D=1+U. Define

    I=(A, min(G,D,delta/2)).                         (1)

If the upper endpoint is at most A, the interval is empty and there is no section of the specified type. On a nonempty I put

    Q(K)=3K^2-2UK+V,
    R(K)=K Q(K)/(delta-2K),

    x(K)= K+R(K)/(K-A),
    y(K)= K+R(K)/(K-B),
    z(K)=-K+(K+R(K))/(G-K),
    w(K)=-K+(K+R(K))/(D-K),
    H(K)=x(K)+y(K)+z(K)+w(K).                       (2)

All four functions are positive on I. For x,y this is immediate. For z, for example,

    z=[K^2+R+(1-G)K]/(G-K)>0,

and similarly for w. Positivity of Q follows from

    Q(A)=A(A-B)>0,
    Q'(K)=6K-2(A+B)>4A-2B>0   for K>A.             (3)

The correspondence is

    K with H(K)=1  <-->  raw normal
             (1/x(K),1/y(K),-1/z(K),-1/w(K)).        (4)

Raw normals differing by a positive common scale represent the same oriented section. The normalization x+y+z+w=1 makes (4) unique.

## 2. Necessity, with every denominator accounted for

For an actual section with positive raw heights (p,q,-r,-s), normalize the reciprocal heights to x+y+z+w=1. Put

    K=xy-zw, N=zw.

The actual centroid formulas, obtained by triangulating the quadrilateral, are

    3a=x/(x+z)+x/(x+w)-x,
    3c=y/(y+z)+y/(y+w)-y,
    3g=z/(z+x)+z/(z+y)-z,
    3d=w/(w+x)+w/(w+y)-w.

Using (x+z)(x+w)=x-K and the three analogous identities gives

    A=(Kx-N)/(x-K),  B=(Ky-N)/(y-K),
    G=(Kz+N+K)/(z+K),  D=(Kw+N+K)/(w+K).           (5)

The denominators are positive. Since A>0, K>0. Since B<=0,

    B-K=(K^2-N)/(y-K)<0,

so N>K^2. The first equation similarly gives A<K. From the other two equations,

    G-K=(N+K-K^2)/(z+K)>0,
    D-K=(N+K-K^2)/(w+K)>0.

Solving (5) therefore entails no zero denominator:

    x=(AK-N)/(A-K), y=(BK-N)/(B-K),
    z=[N+(1-G)K]/(G-K), w=[N+(1-D)K]/(D-K).        (6)

The identities xy=N+K and zw=N yield, after clearing their nonzero denominators,

    E1=N^2-(V+K^2)N+K^2(V+U-K)-VK=0,
    E2=N^2+(-W-K^2+2K)N+K^2(W-U)=0.

Their difference is

    E1-E2=-(2K-delta)N
                 -K[K^2+(delta-2U)K+V].           (7)

If 2K=delta, (7) would force Q(K)=0, contrary to (3), since K>A. Thus this denominator does not vanish. Subtracting K^2 from the resulting expression for N gives

    N-K^2=-K Q(K)/(2K-delta).

The left side and Q(K) are positive, so 2K<delta. Hence K belongs to I and N=K^2+R(K). Substitution in (6) gives exactly (2).

## 3. Sufficiency and an exact quintic certificate

The scalar root equation has an entirely explicit polynomial version. Define

    F(K)=3K^5+(-8U-3V+3W-4)K^4
      +(4U^2+2UV-2UW+4U+6V+4W)K^3
      +(-4UV-4UW+V^2-4V-W^2)K^2
      +(-UV^2+UW^2-V^2+4VW)K+V^2W-VW^2.

Direct common-denominator expansion gives

    H(K)-1=F(K)/[(K-A)(K-B)(G-K)(D-K)(delta-2K)].   (8)

Every denominator in (8) is positive on I. Set N=K^2+R as before. The same expansion gives

    E2=K F(K)/(delta-2K)^2,
    E1-E2=0.                                      (9)

Thus H(K)=1 forces E1=E2=0. Equations (6), whose denominators are nonzero on I, then imply xy=N+K and zw=N. In particular K=xy-zw. All four coordinates are positive by Section 1 and sum to 1 by the root equation. Equations (5) follow by reversing (6); the elementary actual-centroid formulas preceding (5) show that the normal (4) has exactly the prescribed centroid b. No extraneous polynomial root in I remains.

Conversely, Section 2 shows every actual section yields such a root. Distinct roots yield distinct normalized reciprocal heights since xy-zw recovers K, so the correspondence is injective as well as surjective. The leading coefficient of F is always 3; no degree-drop branch is omitted. Equal centroid coordinates, B=0, and repeated roots are all retained.

## 4. Strict convexity of every inverse coordinate

First let f(K)=KQ(K). On K>A,

    f(A)=A^2(A-B)>0,
    f'(A)=A(5A-3B)>0,
    f''(K)=18K-4(A+B)>0.

Hence f is positive, increasing, and strictly convex. Multiplication by the positive increasing convex function 1/(delta-2K) shows that R is positive, increasing, and strictly convex on I.

For x, let K0=delta/2>A. The rational function R/(K-A) has a partial-fraction expansion consisting of an affine function plus

    C_A/(K-A)+C_0/(delta-2K),
    C_A=A Q(A)/(delta-2A)>0,
    C_0=K0 Q(K0)/(K0-A)>0.

The coefficients follow by evaluating the residues at A and K0; the remaining rational function is affine because its numerator has degree three and its denominator degree two. Both displayed reciprocal terms have strictly positive second derivative on I. Thus x''>0.

For y put J(K)=KQ(K)/(K-B). Exact division gives

    J(K)=3K^2+(B-2A)K+B(B-A)+B^2(B-A)/(K-B).

Consequently

    J(A)=A^2>0,
    J'(A)=4A+AB/(A-B)>3A>0,
    J''(K)=6-2B^2(A-B)/(K-B)^3>4.

The final estimate uses K>A and B<=0, so B^2/(A-B)^2<1 (also when B=0). Therefore J is positive, increasing, and strictly convex on I. Since

    y=K+J(K)/(delta-2K),

we obtain y''>0 by the same product rule.

Finally K+R is positive, increasing, and strictly convex. Multiplying it by 1/(G-K) or 1/(D-K), both positive increasing convex on I, and subtracting the affine function K shows z''>0 and w''>0. Therefore

    H''(K)>0 throughout I.                         (10)

## 5. Complete branch count, including collision and endpoint statuses

As K decreases to A, the positive residue C_A/(K-A) makes x, and hence H, tend to infinity. At the upper endpoint of I, either G-K tends to zero, D-K tends to zero, or delta-2K tends to zero. The positive formulas (2), together with Q>0, show H tends to infinity in every case, including coincident upper endpoints.

H is continuous and strictly convex on I. It therefore has one attained interior minimum. If its minimum is above 1 there are no roots; if equal to 1 there is one root, with H'=0 and H''>0; if below 1 there are exactly two roots, with H'<0 at the smaller and H'>0 at the larger. By (8), the unique touching root has multiplicity exactly two as a root of F, and the two distinct roots are simple. There is no escape to an endpoint of I.

For a centroid with one coordinate above 1/3 and all others at most 1/3, this applies to each possible quadrilateral split after placing the noncentral vertex first. The two excluded coordinates of an actual such section are strictly below 1/3 by (5). Thus there are at most six actual strict quadrilateral planes altogether. This count does not forbid three planes from different splits lying in a common pencil; that separate cross-split issue remains outside the theorem.

## 6. The bound two is attained exactly

Take

    b=(56/165,47/225,559/2475,559/2475).

The actual section with raw margins (1/10,2,-1,-1) has this centroid. Here

    I=(1/55,37688/680625),

and the polynomial in Section 3 factors as

    F(K)=(625K-16)(825K-266)^2
              *(13476375K^2+5322240K-131908)
              /1910907861328125.

The two roots in I are

    K1=-1792/9075+266 sqrt(511)/27225,
    K2=16/625.

For an exact interval check, the quadratic factor is strictly increasing on K>=0, is -30685 at K=1/55, and is 41166316/3125 at K=16/625. Thus K1 lies strictly between those two rational numbers; K2 is strictly below the upper endpoint of I. The double root 266/825 lies outside I, and the other quadratic root is negative. Section 3 therefore gives exactly two actual common-centroid sections of the specified split, not just two roots of a relaxation.

## 7. Ordered actual branches in one common normal chart

The three inverse coordinates y,z,w are strictly increasing throughout I. For y this follows directly from the positive increasing function J and the formula in Section 4. For z,

    z'=-1+(1+R')/(G-K)+(K+R)/(G-K)^2>0,

because 0<G-K<1 and R'>0. The same proof applies to w.

Let K_-<K_+ be the two ACTUAL roots. Since H(K_-)=H(K_+)=1, strict increase of y,z,w implies

    x(K_-)>x(K_+),
    y(K_-)<y(K_+), z(K_-)<z(K_+), w(K_-)<w(K_+).

Normalize the raw h entry to 1, writing

    n_-=(1,q_-,-r_-,-s_-),
    n_+=(1,q_+,-r_+,-s_+),
    q=x/y, r=x/z, s=x/w.

Then

    q_->q_+>1, r_->r_+>0, s_->s_+>0.              (11)

The strict q>1 follows independently from (5): Kx>N while Ky<=N, so x>y. Thus the other captured raw coefficient of every actual section of this type is strictly larger than the raw coefficient at the unique noncentral vertex.

An actual third section of a DIFFERENT split with the same centroid, lying on the line through n_- and n_+, cannot lie on the segment between them, where all coordinate signs stay unchanged. Nor can it lie beyond n_- away from n_+, since q, r, s all become still larger and positive there. It must therefore have the form

    n_other=n_++t(n_+-n_-), t>0.                  (12)

Consequently n_+ is the middle point in the positive projective balance of such a triple. This identifies the larger-K section as the uniquely h-excluding actual row after orienting the other two actual rows toward h. The statement is only an orientation/branch constraint; it does not assert that a third actual section exists.

For completeness, suppose the third split captures vertex 3 and still excludes vertex 4. Let Delta_q=q_--q_+, Delta_r=r_--r_+, Delta_s=s_--s_+, all strictly positive. Its required signs and the strict analogue of q>1 imply the exact necessary interval

    max(q_+/Delta_q,(r_++1)/Delta_r)<t<s_+/Delta_s. (13)

If this interval is empty, that specified cross-split triple is impossible. The symmetric condition with r and s interchanged treats capture of vertex 4. No universal emptiness of these intervals is claimed; the actual centroid equations for the third section remain essential.

The ordering in (11) uses the two actual sum-one roots. It must not be replaced by a claim that all three raw-height ratios are monotone over the entire interpolation interval I; Section 4 proves monotonicity of y,z,w, not such a claim about arbitrary ratios away from the actual roots.

## 8. Exact cap data on the two actual branches

At a root write N=zw=K^2+R and S=x+y. For the raw normal (1/x,1/y,-1/z,-1/w), let P be its captured tetrahedral fraction and let f be the density at zero of the corresponding linear combination of four independent mean-one exponential variables. The positive formulas are

    P=N(S-K)/[(x-K)(y-K)],
    f=(N+K)N/[(x-K)(y-K)].                         (14)

For example substituting p=1/x, q=1/y, r=1/z, s=1/w in the usual quadrilateral cap formula gives a numerator

    N^2+N(x+y)(z+w)+N(x^2+xy+y^2)=N(S-K),

where sum(x,y,z,w)=1 and xy=N+K are used. Its denominator is (x+z)(x+w)(y+z)(y+w)=(x-K)(y-K). The exponential convolution formula similarly gives the numerator xyzw=(N+K)N. These are ACTUAL cap quantities at the roots, with no claim that the same expressions describe a centroid-preserving interpolation off those roots.

In terms of U,V,delta and K alone, define

    Z(K)=K^2+(delta-2U)K+V,
    J_0(K)=4K^3+(delta-5U)K^2+(2U^2-delta U)K
                                           +V(delta-U).

Then the actual root values satisfy

    P=Z(K)J_0(K)/Q(K)^2.                           (15)

This follows from R=KQ/(delta-2K), N=KZ/(delta-2K), and

    (delta-2K)(K-A)(K-B)+Q(2K-U)=J_0.

Equations (14)--(15) give exact values for comparing the smaller- and larger-K actual branches. No sign or quantitative upper bound for their probability difference is claimed here.

There is also an exact common-centroid potential. For arbitrary positive reciprocal heights, BEFORE sum-one normalization, let T=x+y+z+w and set

    Psi=log[(x+z)(x+w)(y+z)(y+w)]-log T.

Its logarithmic derivatives are exactly

    partial Psi/partial log x_i=3 b_i(actual).

Thus sections with prescribed centroid b are critical points, modulo common scaling, of Psi-3 sum_i b_i log x_i. Equivalently the exponential zero-density is

    f=xyzw T/[(x+z)(x+w)(y+z)(y+w)],
    partial log f/partial log x_i=1-3b_i(actual).

These identities follow by differentiation of the displayed logarithms and the section-centroid formulas in Section 2. The negative log T term is retained; convexity of this potential is NOT asserted.
